title: Intent-Driven Test Generation
problem: Tests generated by pointing a model at code alone tend to encode implementation details rather than intent — they break on safe refactors, pass right through real regressions, and quietly turn 'internal call order' into a frozen contract nobody meant to freeze.

workflow.detail: Before showing any code, describe in plain language what the function or module is supposed to guarantee to its callers.
Give the model the actual implementation, after the intent is already on the table.
Run the Prompt Template asking for tests keyed to the stated intent and public interface — not internal structure.
Remove any test that asserts on private state, internal call counts, or mock call order — unless that's genuinely part of the contract.
Ask the model to propose one bug it could introduce that the new tests would NOT catch. Decide whether you need another test to close that gap.

promptTemplate:
I need behavior-level tests for the code below. Test the CONTRACT, not the implementation.

INTENT (what this code must guarantee, regardless of how it's implemented):
{{INTENT}}

CODE:
{{CODE}}

TEST FRAMEWORK:
{{FRAMEWORK}}

1. Write tests that verify the stated intent using only the public interface.
2. Do not assert on private state, internal call order, or implementation details.
3. Include at least one edge case implied by the intent (not just the happy path).
4. After the tests, list one behavior-preserving refactor that would NOT break any of them — to prove they test intent, not structure.

variables.name: INTENT
variables.label: Intent / contract
variables.placeholder: e.g. Given a list of orders, returns the total in cents, rounding half up, and never returns negative totals

variables.name: FRAMEWORK
variables.label: Test framework / conventions
variables.placeholder: e.g. Vitest, prefer real objects over mocks

tips: If the model can't state your intent back to you correctly, fix the INTENT field before generating tests — bad tests start from a bad intent description.
For legacy migrations, run this recipe against the OLD implementation first to lock in a safety-net test suite before touching the new one.
Claude and GPT models tend to over-mock by default — explicitly note 'prefer real objects over mocks' in the FRAMEWORK field if that matters to your codebase.
Treat the mutation-check step as the real test of quality: if the model can name an uncaught bug, your suite has a real gap, not just a stylistic one.
